questions.stem: In package com.acme.billing, `public abstract class Ledger` declares `protected void reconcile()`. In package com.acme.audit, `class AuditLedger extends Ledger` has a method `void check(Ledger l, AuditLedger a) { a.reconcile(); l.reconcile(); }`. What does javac do with check?

options.text: It rejects the call on l only, since that call goes through a reference declared as Ledger
options.says: a.reconcile() goes through AuditLedger's own type and compiles; l.reconcile() goes through the base type, which javac rejects with 'reconcile() has protected access in Ledger'

options.text: It rejects the call on a only, since AuditLedger inherits reconcile() without declaring it again
options.says: an inherited protected member is usable through the subclass's own type; declaring it again is not needed

options.text: It accepts both calls, since a subclass may use a protected member on objects of its superclass
options.says: outside the declaring package a subclass reaches a protected instance member only through an expression of its own type or a subtype; l is declared as Ledger

options.text: It rejects both calls, since in another package a protected member may be called on this alone
options.says: another object of the subclass's own type is allowed too, as other.evict(...) on a SessionCache was

origin.section: Protected Opens the Package, and Other Packages Only Through the Subclass's Own Type

questions.stem: `com.shop.pricing.Pricer` has `public long total(long net) { return net + fee(net); }` and `long fee(long net) { return 50; }`. A team in package com.shop.promo writes `public class FreeShippingPricer extends Pricer` declaring `long fee(long net) { return 0; }`, without an annotation. What does `new FreeShippingPricer().total(1_000)` return?

options.text: 1000, since javac would have rejected a fee() in the subclass that did not override
options.says: without @Override javac gives no error and no warning; the subclass method is simply a new method

options.text: 1000, since the call to fee() is dispatched on the FreeShippingPricer object
options.says: dispatch picks among overrides, and a method overrides only a method it can access; Pricer.fee() is package-private in another package

options.text: 1050, since the subclass's fee() is a separate method that total() does not call
options.says: FreeShippingPricer can't see Pricer.fee(), so its fee() overrides nothing and total() calls the original

options.text: 1050, since code inside Pricer binds its calls to Pricer's methods when compiled
options.says: a call to an overridden method does dispatch to the subclass; here nothing is overridden, because the base method is package-private

origin.section: No Modifier Means Package-Private, and a Subclass in Another Package Can't Override It

questions.stem: Version 3 of a plugin library changes `protected void onStart()` in its base class `Plugin` to `public void onStart()`. Your `MetricsPlugin extends Plugin`, written against version 2, declares `protected void onStart()`. You rebuild against version 3. What happens?

options.text: The build fails at MetricsPlugin.onStart(), since a method may not be less accessible than the one it overrides
options.says: an override may widen access but never narrow it; javac reports 'attempting to assign weaker access privileges; was public'

options.text: The build fails where the library calls onStart(), since the library code can no longer reach a protected method
options.says: the library calls onStart() through Plugin, where it is public; the error is on the override itself

options.text: The build succeeds and onStart() stays protected in MetricsPlugin, since each class keeps the level it declares
options.says: code holding a Plugin may call onStart() on any MetricsPlugin, so the override can't be narrower; javac refuses it

options.text: The build succeeds and onStart() becomes public in MetricsPlugin, since an override takes the level of the method it replaces
options.says: an override keeps the level it declares, and javac checks that level against the overridden method; a narrower one is an error

origin.section: An Override May Widen Access but Never Narrow It

questions.stem: On Java 21 an in-house JSON mapper, run from the class path, walks an object's declared fields and for each one does `try { field.setAccessible(true); write(field.get(obj)); } catch (IllegalAccessException e) { /* skip the field */ }`; `write` prints numbers and strings as they are and walks any other value's fields the same way. It is given an application `Order` with a private `long totalCents` and a private `java.time.LocalDate placedOn`. What happens?

options.text: Order's fields are read, then the mapper fails inside placedOn, since the refusal is an exception its catch does not handle
options.says: setAccessible works on the application's own class; on LocalDate's private fields it throws InaccessibleObjectException, which is unchecked and passes the catch

options.text: Order's fields are read, then the mapper leaves out the fields inside placedOn, since the refusal is an exception its catch handles
options.says: the refusal is InaccessibleObjectException, an unchecked exception that a catch for IllegalAccessException (or ReflectiveOperationException) doesn't catch

options.text: All fields are read, LocalDate's included, since setAccessible(true) opens a private field of a JDK class as it does one of Order
options.says: since Java 16 by default, and Java 17 without a switch, setAccessible can't open the JDK's packages unless --add-opens is given

options.text: No field is read, since setAccessible(true) is refused on Java 21 for the private fields of Order as for those of LocalDate
options.says: setAccessible succeeds on the application's own classes on the class path; only the JDK's packages refuse

origin.section: setAccessible Opens Private Members of Class-Path Code, Not of the JDK
